course.title: Mobile App Development with Flutter
course.tagline: Build a real Android and iPhone app with Flutter and Dart, and run it on your own phone.

days.title: What Flutter Is and How to Install It
days.goal: Understand what Flutter is and install it on your computer.

video.title: Flutter Course for Beginners – 37-hour Mobile App Development Tutorial

steps: Go to flutter.dev and download Flutter for your computer.
Install Android Studio, which gives you the Android emulator.
Run flutter doctor in the terminal and fix any item it marks with a cross.
Create a test project with flutter create hello_app and run it.
days.task: Get Flutter installed and run the starter app on an emulator or your phone.
days.challenge: Run flutter doctor again and make every item show a tick.

options: A toolkit for building apps for Android, iPhone, web and desktop from one codebase
quiz.explain: Flutter lets you write one app in Dart and run it on Android, iOS, web and desktop.
Flutter apps are written in Dart, a language made by Google.

options: It checks your setup and tells you what is missing
quiz.explain: flutter doctor checks your Flutter setup and lists anything you still need to install.

days.title: Your First Flutter App
days.goal: Run the starter app and change its text to make it yours.

video.title: Flutter Full Course 2026

steps: Open the starter project in VS Code and find lib/main.dart.
Change the app title and the counter text to your own words.
Save the file and watch hot reload update the app instantly.
Change the theme colour and see it update without restarting.
days.task: Change the starter app into a 'Hello, my name is...' app with your name and a favourite colour.
days.challenge: Add a second text line that shows a short sentence about you.

options: Updating the running app instantly when you save a change, keeping its state
quiz.explain: Hot reload injects your saved changes into the running app without losing where you are.

quiz.q: Where does a Flutter app start?
options: In lib/main.dart, in the main() function
quiz.explain: Every Flutter app starts in lib/main.dart, where main() runs your app.

options: A building block of the user interface, like a button, text or row
quiz.explain: In Flutter everything on screen is a widget: text, buttons, rows, images and more.

days.title: Buttons and Input
days.goal: Let users tap buttons and type into text fields.

video.title: Flutter Full Course 2026 - App Development Course For Beginners

steps: Add an ElevatedButton that prints a message when tapped.
Add a TextField and read what the user types with a controller.
Show what the user typed in a Text widget below the field.
Add a floating action button that increases a counter.
days.task: Build a greeting app: type a name, tap a button, and the app greets you by name.
days.challenge: Add a second button that clears the text field.

options: It runs your code when the button is tapped
quiz.explain: onPressed is the function that runs when the user taps the button.

options: An object that reads and controls what is typed in a text field
quiz.explain: A controller lets you read the text in a field and clear or change it from code.

quiz.q: What is the difference between ElevatedButton and TextButton?
options: ElevatedButton has a raised background, TextButton is flat text
quiz.explain: ElevatedButton is a raised button with a background. TextButton is flat text that acts as a button.

days.title: State: Stateful Widgets
days.goal: Make your app remember things with stateful widgets.

video.title: Flutter Course for Absolute Beginners

steps: Change a widget from StatelessWidget to StatefulWidget.
Add a counter variable in the state class.
Call setState() when the button is tapped to update the counter.
Watch the screen update without restarting the app.
days.task: Build a score counter app with +1 and -1 buttons and a reset button.
days.challenge: Make a light switch app: a button toggles a light bulb icon between on and off.

quiz.q: What is the difference between stateless and stateful widgets?
options: Stateless widgets never change. Stateful widgets hold data that can change and update the screen
quiz.explain: A stateless widget is fixed once built. A stateful widget holds state that can change over time.

options: It tells Flutter the state changed so it rebuilds the widget with new values
quiz.explain: setState() marks the state as changed. Flutter rebuilds the widget so the screen shows the new values.

quiz.q: Where does state live in a stateful widget?
options: In the State class, separate from the widget
quiz.explain: State lives in the State object. The widget is just the configuration; the State holds the changing data.

days.title: Widgets: Text, Images and Icons
days.goal: Show text, pictures and icons in your app.

video.title: Flutter Riverpod Tutorial

steps: Add a Text widget with a big font size and a colour.
Add an Icon widget, like Icons.favorite, with a size and colour.
Add an Image from the internet with Image.network() and a real image URL.
Add an image from your project with Image.asset() after listing it in pubspec.yaml.
days.task: Build a profile screen with a photo, your name, a short bio and three icons.
days.challenge: Add a network image of a place you like and give it a caption.

quiz.q: What does a Text widget do?
options: It shows a line of text on the screen
quiz.explain: Text shows words. You set its content and style, like size and colour.

options: It lists your app's name, dependencies and assets like images and fonts
quiz.explain: pubspec.yaml is your app's config file: its name, packages it uses, and assets like images.

quiz.q: What is the difference between Image.network and Image.asset?
options: network loads from a URL, asset loads a file inside your project
quiz.explain: Image.network fetches a picture from the internet. Image.asset uses a file you bundled with the app.

days.title: Layout: Rows, Columns and Containers
days.goal: Arrange widgets on the screen with rows, columns and containers.

video.title: Firebase Authentication and Flutter Full Course 2020

steps: Put two Text widgets in a Row so they sit side by side.
Put three widgets in a Column so they stack top to bottom.
Wrap a widget in a Container and give it padding, margin and a background colour.
Use SizedBox to add space between widgets.
days.task: Build a business card screen: a column with a name, a job title, a row of icons and space between each part.
days.challenge: Make a row of three coloured boxes with equal space between them.

options: It puts widgets side by side
It stacks widgets top to bottom
quiz.explain: Column arranges its children vertically, one below the other.

options: It puts widgets side by side in a line
quiz.explain: Row arranges its children horizontally, one next to the other.

options: It holds one child and lets you set padding, margin, colour and size around it
quiz.explain: Container wraps one child and adds decoration like padding, margin, background colour and borders.

days.title: Project 1: Business Card App
days.goal: Build a complete business card app with layout, images and state.

video.title: Firebase Authentication and Flutter Full Course 2020

steps: Make a card screen with a photo, name, job title and contact details.
Use Column, Row and Container to lay it out neatly.
Add a button that shows or hides the phone number.
Style it with colours, rounded corners and good spacing.
days.task: Finish the business card app with your real details and run it on your phone.
days.challenge: Add a second card for a friend with different details, using the same layout.

quiz.q: Why use a Column for a business card?
options: A card stacks its parts top to bottom: photo, name, title, contact
quiz.explain: A business card reads top to bottom, which is exactly what a Column does.

quiz.q: What does setState() do when the button is tapped?
options: It rebuilds the widget so the phone number appears or disappears
quiz.explain: setState() tells Flutter to rebuild with the new state, so the hidden part shows or hides.

quiz.q: Why use a Container for the card?
options: To give the card padding, a background colour and rounded corners
quiz.explain: Container adds the padding, colour and rounded corners that make a plain column look like a card.

project.title: Business Card App
project.brief: Build a business card app in Flutter: a photo, name, job title and contact details laid out neatly with Column, Row and Container, plus a button that shows or hides the phone number.
checks: The card shows a photo, name, job title and contact details.
The layout uses Column, Row and Container.
A button shows or hides the phone number.
The card has colours, rounded corners and good spacing.
The app runs on an emulator or a real phone.
The code is tidy with widgets split into small pieces.

days.title: Dart Basics 1: Variables, Types and Functions
days.goal: Learn the Dart basics you need for Flutter: variables, types and functions.

video.title: Flutter & Firebase App Tutorial #2 - Firebase Setup

steps: Declare a variable with var, String, int and double, and print each one.
Write a function that takes two numbers and returns their sum.
Use string interpolation with $name to put a value inside text.
Try final and const and notice they cannot be changed.
days.task: Write a small Dart program that stores a name and age and prints a greeting.
days.challenge: Write a function that takes a price and a discount percent and returns the final price.

options: The programming language Flutter apps are written in
quiz.explain: Dart is the language behind Flutter. You write your app logic and widgets in Dart.

quiz.q: What does final mean in Dart?
options: The variable can be set once and never changed after
quiz.explain: final means the value is set once and locked. Use it for values that should not change.

quiz.q: How do you put a variable inside a string in Dart?
quiz.explain: Dart uses $name for a variable and ${...} for an expression inside a string.

days.title: Dart Basics 2: Lists, Maps and Loops
days.goal: Use Dart lists, maps and loops to handle data in your app.

video.title: Flutter Firebase Tutorial 2026: Complete Auth + Firestore Integration

steps: Make a list of five names and print each one with a for loop.
Make a map for a person with name and age keys, and print the name.
Use .map() to turn a list of numbers into a list of doubled numbers.
Use .where() to keep only the items that match a condition.
days.task: Make a list of five products as maps and print each product's name and price.
days.challenge: Filter a list of numbers to only the even ones and print them.

quiz.q: What is a list in Dart?
options: An ordered collection of items, like [1, 2, 3]
quiz.explain: A list holds items in order. You read them by position, starting at 0.

quiz.q: What is a map in Dart?
options: A collection of key-value pairs, like {'name': 'Ada'}
quiz.explain: A map stores named values. You read them by key, like person['name'].

options: It returns a new list with only the items that pass your test
quiz.explain: .where() keeps only the items where your test is true.

days.title: Lists: ListView
days.goal: Show long lists that scroll with ListView.

video.title: Flutter Tutorial For Beginners in 13 Hours

steps: Make a list of ten items in a Dart list.
Show them with ListView.builder so only visible items are built.
Give each item a ListTile with a title and a subtitle.
Add an icon at the start of each row.
days.task: Build a contacts list with ten people, each with a name and a phone number.
days.challenge: Make the list show 50 items and notice it still scrolls smoothly.

options: It builds every item at once
It builds only the items on screen, which keeps long lists fast
quiz.explain: ListView.builder creates items lazily, only when they scroll into view, so long lists stay smooth.

options: A ready-made row with a title, subtitle and icons, used in lists
quiz.explain: ListTile is a pre-built list row with a leading icon, a title and a subtitle.

quiz.q: Why is a builder better than a plain ListView for long lists?
options: It only builds visible items, so memory stays low
quiz.explain: Building only visible items saves memory and time when the list is long.

days.title: Navigation: Moving Between Screens
days.goal: Move between screens with Navigator and pass data along.

video.title: Flutter Course for Beginners – 37-hour Mobile App Development Tutorial

steps: Make a second screen widget in a new file.
Push to it with Navigator.push() and a MaterialPageRoute.
Pass a name to the second screen and show it there.
Go back with Navigator.pop() or the back button.
days.task: Build an app with a home screen and a details screen that shows the item you tapped.
days.challenge: Add a back button on the details screen that returns to the home screen.

options: It opens a new screen on top of the current one
quiz.explain: push() adds a new screen to the stack. The back button pops it off to return.

quiz.q: How do you pass data to a new screen?
options: Give the screen's constructor a value, like DetailsScreen(name: 'Ada')
quiz.explain: You pass data through the screen widget's constructor when you create the route.

options: It closes the current screen and goes back to the one below
quiz.explain: pop() removes the top screen from the stack, returning to the previous screen.

days.title: Forms and Validation
days.goal: Build forms that check user input before accepting it.

video.title: Flutter Full Course 2026

steps: Wrap your fields in a Form widget with a GlobalKey.
Add a validator to each field that returns an error message for bad input.
Check the email contains @ and the password is at least 8 characters.
Show a success message when the form is valid and submitted.
days.task: Build a sign-up form with name, email and password validation.
days.challenge: Add a rule that the two password fields must match.

options: It checks the field's value and returns an error message or null when it is fine
quiz.explain: A validator runs when you check the form. It returns an error message for bad input, or null when the input is fine.

quiz.q: What is a GlobalKey for a form?
options: A key that lets you check the whole form and run all its validators at once
quiz.explain: The form key gives you access to the form state, so you can call validate() on all fields together.

quiz.q: Why validate before accepting a form?
options: To stop bad data being saved and to tell users exactly what to fix
quiz.explain: Validation catches mistakes early and shows a clear message, instead of saving bad data.

days.title: Gestures and User Interaction
days.goal: React to taps, swipes and long presses with gesture widgets.

video.title: Flutter Full Course 2026 - App Development Course For Beginners

steps: Wrap a widget in GestureDetector and print a message on tap.
Add onDoubleTap to run different code on a double tap.
Add onLongPress to show a menu when the user holds a widget.
Use InkWell on a card so it shows a ripple effect when tapped.
days.task: Build a photo grid where tapping a photo opens it bigger and long-pressing shows its name.
days.challenge: Make a card that changes colour when you tap it and back when you tap again.

options: It detects taps, swipes and other gestures on its child
quiz.explain: GestureDetector watches its child for gestures like tap, double tap and long press, and runs your code.

quiz.q: What is the difference between GestureDetector and InkWell?
options: InkWell adds a ripple effect on tap and needs a Material ancestor
quiz.explain: InkWell is like GestureDetector but shows a ripple, which is the standard Material touch feedback.

options: To offer extra actions, like delete or share, without cluttering the screen
quiz.explain: Long press hides extra actions until needed, keeping the screen clean.

days.title: Project 2: Notes App
days.goal: Build a notes app with lists, navigation and local storage.

video.title: Flutter Course for Absolute Beginners

steps: Make a home screen that lists notes with title and a short preview.
Tapping a note opens an edit screen where you can change it.
Add a button to create a new note.
Save notes to the device with shared_preferences so they survive closing the app.
days.task: Finish the notes app with at least three notes and test that they survive a restart.
days.challenge: Add a delete button with a confirm dialog before deleting a note.

quiz.q: Why save notes to the device?
options: So notes are still there after the app closes
quiz.explain: State disappears when the app closes. Saving to the device keeps notes between visits.

options: A simple way to save small data like settings and lists on the device
quiz.explain: shared_preferences stores small key-value data on the device, like settings or a list of notes.

quiz.q: Why use a confirm dialog before deleting?
options: To stop accidental deletes of something the user may want
quiz.explain: A confirm dialog prevents losing a note by accident, which is hard to undo.

project.title: Notes App with Local Storage
project.brief: Build a notes app: a home screen lists notes, tapping one opens an edit screen, a button adds new notes, and notes are saved on the device with shared_preferences so they survive closing the app.
checks: The home screen lists notes with title and preview.
Tapping a note opens an edit screen.
A button creates a new note.
Notes are saved on the device and load after a restart.
A note can be deleted, with a confirm dialog first.
The list scrolls smoothly with ListView.

days.title: State Management with Provider
days.goal: Share state across screens with the Provider package.

video.title: Flutter Riverpod Tutorial

steps: Add provider to pubspec.yaml and run flutter pub get.
Make a ChangeNotifier class that holds a list and methods to add and remove.
Wrap your app in ChangeNotifierProvider.
Read the data in a widget with Provider.of or Consumer, and call notifyListeners() after changes.
days.task: Build a shopping list app where the list lives in a Provider and two screens can read it.
days.challenge: Add a counter in a Provider and show it on two different screens.

options: A package that shares state with many widgets without passing it down by hand
quiz.explain: Provider makes a value available to the whole widget tree below it, so any widget can read it.

options: It tells widgets that listen to the provider to rebuild with the new data
quiz.explain: After you change the data, notifyListeners() tells listening widgets to rebuild.

quiz.q: Why use Provider instead of passing data down manually?
options: It avoids passing data through many layers that do not need it
quiz.explain: Provider skips prop drilling: any widget can read the shared state directly.

days.title: State Management with Riverpod
days.goal: Try Riverpod, a modern and safe way to manage state.

video.title: Firebase Authentication and Flutter Full Course 2020

steps: Add flutter_riverpod to pubspec.yaml and run flutter pub get.
Wrap your app in ProviderScope.
Make a StateProvider for a counter and read it with ref.watch().
Change it with ref.read() and a button.
days.task: Rewrite your counter app using Riverpod instead of setState.
days.challenge: Make a list provider that holds tasks and lets you add and remove them.

options: A modern state management package that is safe and testable, built by the Provider author
quiz.explain: Riverpod is a newer state package. It does not depend on the widget tree, which makes it easier to test.

options: It reads a provider's value and rebuilds the widget when it changes
quiz.explain: ref.watch() subscribes to a provider. When the provider's value changes, the widget rebuilds.

quiz.q: What is the difference between ref.watch and ref.read?
options: watch rebuilds the widget on change, read just takes the value once without listening
quiz.explain: watch listens and rebuilds. read takes the current value once, which is right for button taps.

days.title: Fetching Data from an API
days.goal: Load real data from the internet and show it in your app.

video.title: Firebase Authentication and Flutter Full Course 2020

steps: Add the http package to pubspec.yaml.
Use http.get() to fetch a list from a public API.
Turn the JSON reply into Dart objects with jsonDecode.
Show a loading spinner while waiting and the list when it arrives.
days.task: Build an app that fetches a list of posts from a public API and shows their titles.
days.challenge: Add a pull-to-refresh that fetches the data again.

options: A widget that builds different things while a future is loading, done or failed
quiz.explain: FutureBuilder watches a Future and shows a spinner while loading, the data when done, or an error when it fails.

options: It turns a JSON string into Dart maps and lists
It saves JSON to a file
quiz.explain: jsonDecode parses JSON text into Dart data you can work with.

options: So the user knows data is coming instead of seeing a blank screen
quiz.explain: Data takes time to arrive. A spinner tells the user something is happening.

days.title: Firebase Setup
days.goal: Connect your app to Firebase, Google's backend for apps.

video.title: Flutter & Firebase App Tutorial #2 - Firebase Setup

steps: Create a Firebase project at console.firebase.google.com.
Add an Android app and download the google-services.json file into your project.
Add firebase_core to pubspec.yaml and initialise Firebase in main().
Run the app and check Firebase connects without errors.
days.task: Set up Firebase for your notes app project and confirm it connects.
days.challenge: Add the iOS app in Firebase too, if you have a Mac.

options: Google's backend service for apps: login, database, storage and more
quiz.explain: Firebase gives your app a ready-made backend: user login, a live database, file storage and notifications.

options: It starts Firebase in your app so other Firebase services can work
quiz.explain: firebase_core initialises Firebase. Every other Firebase package needs it first.

options: A config file that tells your app which Firebase project it belongs to
quiz.explain: google-services.json holds your Firebase project's settings. Your app reads it when it starts.

days.title: Firebase Login
days.goal: Let users sign up and log in with email and password.

video.title: Flutter Firebase Tutorial 2026: Complete Auth + Firestore Integration

steps: Add firebase_auth to pubspec.yaml.
Make a sign-up screen that creates a user with createUserWithEmailAndPassword.
Make a login screen that signs in with signInWithEmailAndPassword.
Show a different home screen when a user is logged in.
days.task: Add login and sign-up to your notes app so each user sees only their own notes.
days.challenge: Add a logout button and a 'forgot password' link.

options: Firebase's service for user sign-up, login and logout
quiz.explain: Firebase Auth handles user accounts: sign-up, login, logout and password reset, without you building a server.

quiz.q: Why use Firebase Auth instead of building your own login?
options: It handles passwords safely, including hashing and reset emails, which is hard to do well yourself
quiz.explain: Passwords must be stored safely. Firebase Auth does the hard security work for you.

quiz.q: How do you know if a user is logged in?
options: Check FirebaseAuth.instance.currentUser, or listen to authStateChanges()
quiz.explain: currentUser holds the logged-in user, or null. authStateChanges() tells you live when login state changes.

days.title: Cloud Firestore: Saving Data Online
days.goal: Store data in the cloud with Cloud Firestore so it syncs across devices.

video.title: Flutter Tutorial For Beginners in 13 Hours

steps: Add cloud_firestore to pubspec.yaml.
Save a note to a collection with add() and read it back with get().
Listen to changes live with snapshots() so the list updates when data changes.
Store each user's notes under their own user id.
days.task: Move your notes app from local storage to Firestore so notes sync online.
days.challenge: Add a timestamp to each note and sort the list by newest first.

options: Firebase's cloud database that stores data in collections and documents and syncs live
quiz.explain: Firestore is a cloud database. Data is stored as documents in collections, and apps can listen for live updates.

options: A group of documents, like a table of notes
quiz.explain: A collection holds documents. A 'notes' collection holds one document per note.

quiz.q: Why listen with snapshots() instead of fetching once?
options: It updates the app live whenever the data changes, on any device
quiz.explain: snapshots() streams changes, so the list updates the moment data changes, without refreshing.

days.title: Project 3: Complete App with Login and Cloud Data
days.goal: Build a full app with login, cloud data and a polished design.

video.title: Flutter Course for Beginners – 37-hour Mobile App Development Tutorial

steps: Plan the app: screens, data and what each screen does.
Add Firebase login so each user has their own account.
Store the app's data in Firestore under each user's id.
Add a polished theme, animations and a loading state.
days.task: Finish the full app and test it with two different user accounts.
days.challenge: Add a settings screen where the user can change their display name.

quiz.q: Why store data under each user's id?
options: So each user sees only their own data, not everyone else's
quiz.explain: Separating data by user id keeps each person's data private and stops users seeing each other's items.

options: Login, cloud data, good design and handling of loading and errors
quiz.explain: A complete app handles real users: login, saved data, good design, loading states and errors.

options: To prove each user only sees their own data
quiz.explain: Two accounts prove the data separation works: each account should see only its own items.

project.title: Complete App with Login and Cloud Data
project.brief: Build a full app with Firebase login, data stored in Cloud Firestore under each user's id, a polished theme and animations, and loading and error states.
checks: Users can sign up and log in with email and password.
Data is stored in Firestore under each user's id.
Each user sees only their own data.
The app has a polished theme and at least one animation.
Loading and error states show at the right times.
The app runs without errors on a real phone or emulator.

days.title: Push Notifications
days.goal: Send notifications to users with Firebase Cloud Messaging.

video.title: Flutter Full Course 2026

steps: Add firebase_messaging to pubspec.yaml.
Ask the user for permission to send notifications.
Get the device token and print it to the console.
Handle a notification that arrives while the app is open.
days.task: Add notifications to your app and test one with the Firebase console.
days.challenge: Show a local notification when a note reminder time arrives.

options: Firebase's service for sending push notifications to phones
quiz.explain: FCM delivers push notifications to Android and iPhone apps, even when the app is closed.

options: A unique address for one phone that lets Firebase send it notifications
quiz.explain: Each phone gets a token. Firebase uses it to know which phone a notification should go to.

options: Because phones require the user's OK before an app can send notifications
quiz.explain: Phones block notifications until the user allows them, so you must ask first.

days.title: App Icon, Splash Screen and Polish
days.goal: Give your app a proper icon and a splash screen before you show it to anyone.

video.title: Flutter Full Course 2026 - App Development Course For Beginners

steps: Add flutter_launcher_icons to pubspec.yaml and set your icon image.
Run the command to generate icons for Android and iOS.
Add a splash screen with your app name and colours.
Check the icon and splash screen on a real phone.
days.task: Make an app icon for your notes app and set it as the launcher icon.
days.challenge: Design a simple splash screen with your app's name and a colour that matches your theme.

options: The icon users tap on their home screen to open your app
quiz.explain: The launcher icon is your app's picture on the home screen. It is the first thing users see.

options: The first screen that shows briefly while your app loads
quiz.explain: A splash screen shows your logo or name while the app starts, so users do not see a blank screen.

quiz.q: Why polish the icon and splash screen?
options: Because they are the first impression of your app and make it look professional
quiz.explain: The icon and splash screen are what users see first. Good ones make your app feel real and trustworthy.

days.title: Working with Images and Media
days.goal: Let users pick photos from the gallery or take new ones with the camera.

video.title: Flutter Course for Absolute Beginners

steps: Add image_picker to pubspec.yaml and run flutter pub get.
Use ImagePicker to let the user choose a photo from the gallery.
Show the chosen photo in an Image.file widget.
Let the user take a new photo with the camera.
days.task: Add a profile photo to your notes app that the user can pick from the gallery.
days.challenge: Save the photo's path so it still shows after the app restarts.

options: A package that lets your app pick photos from the gallery or camera
quiz.explain: image_picker opens the gallery or camera and returns the photo the user chose.

options: A photo stored as a file on the device
quiz.explain: Image.file displays a picture from a file path on the device, like a photo the user just picked.

quiz.q: Why ask permission before using the camera?
options: Because phones require the user's OK before an app can use the camera or photos
quiz.explain: Phones block camera and photo access until the user allows it, so you must ask first.

days.title: Styling and Themes
days.goal: Give your app a consistent look with themes, colours and fonts.

video.title: Flutter Riverpod Tutorial

steps: Set a ThemeData in MaterialApp with a primary colour and font.
Use Theme.of(context) to read the theme colours in a widget.
Add a custom font: list it in pubspec.yaml and use it in the theme.
Add a dark mode toggle that switches the theme.
days.task: Style your notes app with a clean theme, a custom font and good spacing.
days.challenge: Make the app look good in both light and dark mode.

options: A set of colours, fonts and styles that your whole app shares
quiz.explain: ThemeData holds your app's design choices in one place, so every screen looks consistent.

quiz.q: Why use the theme instead of setting colours everywhere?
options: So one change updates the whole app and the design stays consistent
quiz.explain: One theme file means one place to change colours. Every screen follows it automatically.

quiz.q: How do you add a custom font?
options: Put the font file in assets, list it in pubspec.yaml, and name it in the theme
quiz.explain: Fonts go in an assets folder, are listed in pubspec.yaml, and are named in ThemeData.

days.title: Animations
days.goal: Add motion to your app with simple animations.

video.title: Firebase Authentication and Flutter Full Course 2020

steps: Use AnimatedContainer to smoothly change size or colour when state changes.
Add a Hero animation so an image grows when you open its detail screen.
Use a simple FadeTransition or AnimatedOpacity to fade a widget in.
Add a loading animation while data is being fetched.
days.task: Add an animation to your notes app: cards fade in when the list loads.
days.challenge: Make a button that grows slightly when tapped.

options: It smoothly changes its size, colour or shape when its values change
quiz.explain: AnimatedContainer animates between its old and new values over a short time, instead of jumping.

options: An animation that moves a widget from one screen to the next, like an image growing into a detail page
quiz.explain: A Hero with the same tag on two screens animates the widget between them, which looks smooth and polished.

options: To guide the user's eye and make the app feel smooth and alive
quiz.explain: Small animations show what changed and where things went, which makes the app feel polished.

days.title: Testing Your App
days.goal: Test your app so you can change it with confidence.

video.title: Firebase Authentication and Flutter Full Course 2020

steps: Write a unit test for a function that formats a date or calculates a total.
Write a widget test that checks a button appears on the screen.
Tap the button in the test and check the counter changes.
Run flutter test and read the pass and fail results.
days.task: Write tests for your notes app: one for adding a note and one for deleting it.
days.challenge: Write a test that checks an error message appears for an empty note.

options: A test of the whole app
A test of one small function or piece of logic on its own
quiz.explain: A unit test checks one function in isolation, like a date formatter or a total calculator.

options: A test that builds a widget and checks it shows and behaves correctly
quiz.explain: A widget test renders your widget, checks what it shows, and simulates taps.

options: So you can change code safely, knowing tests will catch breaks
quiz.explain: Tests catch regressions. When you refactor, green tests tell you nothing broke.

days.title: Publishing Your App
days.goal: Prepare your app for the Play Store and App Store.

video.title: Flutter & Firebase App Tutorial #2 - Firebase Setup

steps: Set the app name, icon and version in pubspec.yaml and the platform files.
Build a release version with flutter build apk for Android.
Test the release build on a real phone.
Read the store requirements for screenshots, description and privacy policy.
days.task: Build a release version of your app and install it on a real phone.
days.challenge: Make an app icon and a feature image for the store listing.

quiz.q: What does flutter build apk do?
options: It builds a release Android app file you can install or upload to the Play Store
quiz.explain: flutter build apk creates an installable release file for Android, optimised for real users.

quiz.q: Why test the release build on a real phone?
options: Because release builds can behave differently from debug builds, and real phones catch real problems
quiz.explain: Release builds are optimised and signed differently. Testing on a real phone catches problems debug mode hides.

quiz.q: What does a store listing need?
options: An icon, screenshots, a description and a privacy policy
quiz.explain: Stores need an icon, screenshots, a description and a privacy policy before they list your app.

days.title: Performance and Polish
days.goal: Make your app fast and smooth before you show it to anyone.

video.title: Flutter Firebase Tutorial 2026: Complete Auth + Firestore Integration

steps: Use const constructors where you can, so Flutter skips rebuilding those widgets.
Keep build() methods small and fast.
Use ListView.builder for long lists instead of building everything at once.
Check the app with the Flutter performance tools and fix the slowest part.
days.task: Find the slowest screen in your app and make it faster.
days.challenge: Remove unused packages from pubspec.yaml and rebuild.

options: They let Flutter skip rebuilding widgets that never change, which saves time
quiz.explain: A const widget never changes, so Flutter can reuse it instead of rebuilding it every time.

options: build() runs every time the widget rebuilds, so slow work there makes the app lag
quiz.explain: build() runs on every rebuild. Heavy work inside it, like fetching data, makes the app stutter.

quiz.q: What is the first step to fixing a slow app?
options: Measure with the performance tools to find the real slow part
quiz.explain: Measure first. Guessing wastes time; the tools show exactly which widget is slow.

days.title: Capstone Prep: Plan Your App
days.goal: Review everything, pick your capstone app and plan your demo.

video.title: Flutter Tutorial For Beginners in 13 Hours

steps: List all the apps you built in 30 days and pick your favourite.
Write a short plan: the problem, the screens, the data and the backend.
Practise explaining your app in simple words, as if to a friend.
Record a short video or write a short post showing your app running on a phone.
days.task: Write your capstone plan and a one-minute explanation of your app.
days.challenge: Show your app to one person and note their questions, then improve your explanation.

quiz.q: What makes a good capstone app?
options: One real problem solved well, with login, cloud data and a working demo
quiz.explain: A good capstone solves one real problem clearly, with real users, saved data and a demo that works.

options: Because explaining simply proves you truly understand it
quiz.explain: If you can explain your app in simple words, you really understand it. That is what employers look for.

quiz.q: What should your capstone plan include?
options: The problem, the screens, the data, the backend and how you will show it
quiz.explain: A plan covers the problem, the screens, the data and backend, and how you will present it.

capstone.title: Build and Publish a Real Mobile App
capstone.brief: Build a complete mobile app that solves a real problem: a budget tracker, a habit tracker, a small shop or a study planner. It must have Firebase login, cloud data in Firestore, at least three screens, a clean design, and a release build you can install on a phone. Share the code on GitHub with a README and a short demo video.
checks: The app solves one real problem and you can explain the problem in one sentence.
It has at least three screens with navigation between them.
Users log in with Firebase Auth and see only their own data.
Data is stored in Cloud Firestore and syncs online.
It has a clean theme, good spacing and at least one animation.
A release build installs and runs on a real phone.
You can show a live demo on a phone and explain how it works in simple words.
deliverables: A release build (APK) that installs on a phone.
A public GitHub repository link with the code.
A README.md explaining the problem, the features and how to run it.
A short demo video of the app running on a real phone.
